common_name: Mount Airy Fothergilla (Award-Winning Fragrant Bottlebrush Shrub)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring in moist, well-drained, acidic soil in partial shade to full sun; Mount Airy tolerates a wider range of soil and moisture conditions than the wild species and produces its best fall color and heaviest bloom in full sun.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic soil (pH 4.5–6.0) in partial shade to full sun, and mulch to keep roots cool and evenly moist through summer heat. Mount Airy is a selection discovered at the Mount Airy Arboretum in Cincinnati, thought to be a hybrid between dwarf and large fothergilla, combining the compact, tidy habit of the smaller species with exceptionally heavy flowering and outstanding fall color. In April, before the leaves emerge, the shrub is covered in fragrant, honey-scented, bottlebrush-like white flower spikes made up of dense stamens, followed by attractive blue-green summer foliage that turns a spectacular blend of yellow, orange, and scarlet — often several colors on a single leaf — in fall. Its reliable performance, compact size, and multi-season interest have made it one of the most widely planted and highly rated fothergilla selections available, suited to a shrub border, woodland edge, or foundation planting. Requires minimal pruning; simply remove dead or crossing wood after flowering if shaping is needed.

common_name: Pride of Augusta Carolina Jessamine (Double-Flowered Evergreen Vine)

planting.note: Plant container vines in spring or fall in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade against a trellis, arbor, or fence; Pride of Augusta blooms most heavily in full sun but tolerates partial shade with somewhat reduced flowering.

directions: Plant against a sturdy trellis, arbor, mailbox post, or fence in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade, and train young vines onto their support until the twining stems take hold on their own. Pride of Augusta is a heritage double-flowered selection of Carolina jessamine, the southeastern native evergreen vine, bearing fully double, ruffled, deep golden-yellow flowers with a sweet fragrance that smother the vine in late winter to early spring, a showier and longer-lasting display than the single flowers of the standard species. Its glossy, twining evergreen foliage provides year-round cover for a fence or arbor even when not in bloom, and once established the vine is highly drought-tolerant and easy-care, asking for little beyond an annual light pruning after flowering to control size and shape. All parts of the plant are toxic if ingested, so site it away from areas where livestock or small children might be tempted to chew the foliage or flowers.
sources: The Antique Rose Emporium and heritage vine nursery records

common_name: Emerald Snow Loropetalum (Cold-Hardy White-Flowered Green Fringe Flower)

planting.note: Plant container plants in spring in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; Emerald Snow was bred for improved cold hardiness compared to older white-flowered loropetalum selections, making it more reliable in the northern part of the Gulf South.

directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; Emerald Snow is a white-flowered Loropetalum chinense selection that departs from the more familiar burgundy-leaved, pink-flowered loropetalum cultivars, instead pairing clean green evergreen foliage with abundant, fringe-petaled white flowers in spring and scattered rebloom later in the season. Bred for improved winter hardiness relative to older white-flowered selections, it holds up well through colder snaps common in the northern Gulf South while retaining the vigorous, adaptable growth habit typical of the species. Its all-green foliage makes it a versatile companion for gardens that already feature plenty of burgundy loropetalum, offering contrast and a softer, more traditional look for a hedge, foundation planting, or mixed border. Prune lightly right after the main spring bloom to shape, since later pruning removes developing flower buds.
sources: Southern Living Plant Collection — Loropetalum cultivar notes

common_name: Center of Attention Distylium (Upright Burgundy New-Growth Evergreen Shrub)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist to moderately dry, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Center of Attention grows taller and more upright than most distylium cultivars, making it useful as a screen or informal hedge without frequent pruning.

directions: Plant in moist to moderately dry, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade, spacing plants to allow the upright, vase-shaped form to develop into a screen or informal hedge without crowding. Center of Attention is a First Editions distylium selection with a notably taller, more upright habit than typical mounding distylium cultivars, producing burgundy-red new growth that matures to glossy dark green, along with small maroon flowers along the stems in late winter. Like other distylium, it shares the species' rare tolerance for both full sun and full shade, wet or dry soils, and strong resistance to the pests and diseases that trouble many broadleaf evergreens in humid Gulf South summers, along with being seldom browsed by deer. Its taller, narrower form makes it particularly useful as a living privacy screen or vertical accent where a low, spreading distylium would be the wrong shape, and it needs only occasional shaping to maintain its natural upright form.
sources: First Editions Shrubs & Trees — Center of Attention variety notes

planting.note: Plant container or balled-and-burlapped trees in spring or fall in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade; Satomi flowers most heavily and develops the deepest pink bract color with a half-day or more of direct sun.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade, and water deeply and regularly through the first two years to establish before the tree can tolerate brief dry spells. Satomi is a classic pink-bracted Kousa dogwood cultivar, bearing large, star-shaped, deep rose-pink flower bracts in late spring after the leaves have emerged, later than native flowering dogwood, followed by raspberry-like red fruit in late summer that attracts birds, and finishing the season with reddish-purple fall foliage color. Kousa dogwoods bloom on a delay compared to native Cornus florida and show much better resistance to the anthracnose and borer problems that plague native dogwood in humid climates, making Satomi a reliable substitute where disease pressure has made native dogwood difficult to grow. Its attractive, exfoliating bark adds winter interest once the tree matures, and it works well as a specimen tree, understory planting, or focal point near a patio where its multi-season display can be enjoyed up close.
